passages.t: Daniel's excellence, and a plot against his prayers
passages.happening:
Darius appoints 120 satraps to rule his kingdom, with three administrators over them, Daniel among them (verses 1-2). ‘Soon, by his extraordinary spirit, Daniel distinguished himself among the administrators and satraps’ (verse 3), and the king plans to set him over the whole kingdom.

The other officials look for a charge against him, but they find none, ‘because he was trustworthy, and no negligence or corruption was found in him’ (verse 4). So they say, ‘We will never find any charge against this Daniel, unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God’ (verse 5).

They go to the king together and propose a decree: for thirty days, anyone who prays to any god or man except the king will be thrown into the den of lions (verses 6-7). They ask him to sign it so that it cannot be changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians (verse 8). ‘Therefore King Darius signed the written decree’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The kingdom has passed from Babylon to the Medes and Persians, but the position of God's people has not changed. They still live under a foreign king whose laws can turn against them. Daniel, now past eighty if the book's dates are followed, serves the new government with the same integrity he showed the old.

The Persians ruled through satraps, provincial governors, with other officials under them. Herodotus counts about twenty satrapies in the time of Darius I, so the 120 here are often taken as a wider term for regional officials. The rule that a royal decree could not be revoked appears also in Esther, as a law of Persia and Media. No Persian source states it in those words, and some think it reflects a court custom that the king's word was final.

The officials knew Daniel's faithfulness was the only place they could catch him. That is the highest praise the chapter gives him. His enemies could find nothing against him except his loyalty to God. The decree flatters the king by making him the only channel to heaven for a month. Darius signs it without seeing the trap.
passages.later: The same law of the Medes and Persians binds King Ahasuerus in Esther: ‘a decree that is written in the name of the king and sealed with the royal signet ring cannot be revoked’ (Esther 8:8). A psalm describes life among such enemies: ‘My soul is among the lions; I lie down with ravenous beasts’ (Psalm 57:4).
passages.asks: Daniel's enemies could find no fault in him except his faithfulness to God. Ask what your critics would find if they looked as hard. And ask what you would want people to say was the only charge they could bring against you.

passages.t: Daniel prays as before, and is thrown to the lions
passages.happening:
‘Now when Daniel learned that the document had been signed, he went into his house, where the windows of his upper room opened toward Jerusalem, and three times a day he got down on his knees, prayed, and gave thanks to his God, just as he had done before’ (verse 10).

The men find him praying and go straight to the king. They remind him of the decree, and the king agrees that it stands (verses 11-12). Then they tell him that Daniel, ‘one of the exiles from Judah’, still prays three times a day (verse 13).

The king is deeply distressed. He sets his mind on saving Daniel and works until sundown to rescue him (verse 14). But the men remind him that no decree of the king can be changed (verse 15). So Daniel is thrown into the den. The king says to him, ‘May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you’ (verse 16).

A stone is placed over the mouth of the den and sealed with the king's ring and his nobles' rings (verse 17). The king goes back to his palace and spends the night fasting, with no entertainment, unable to sleep (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Daniel does not hide, and he does not make a show. He does what he had always done. He prays toward Jerusalem because Solomon's prayer at the temple's dedication had asked God to hear his people when they prayed toward the land, the city and the temple from the land of their captivity. Daniel prays that way though the temple lies in ruins. Praying three times a day matches a psalm and became Jewish practice.

Notice that he gives thanks. His prayer under threat is not only a plea for help. It is thanksgiving.

The chapter pairs with chapter 3. There the test was a command to do what God forbids. Here it is a command not to do what God requires. The first hearers, under foreign rule, were being prepared for both.

The king is a tragic figure. He loves Daniel and cannot save him, because he has bound himself by his own law. His accusers call him one of the exiles from Judah, much as Belshazzar did. To them, after a lifetime of service, he is still a foreigner.
passages.later: Solomon had prayed that when the people ‘pray to You in the direction of the land that You gave to their fathers, the city You have chosen’, God would hear (1 Kings 8:48-49). A psalmist prays ‘Morning, noon, and night’ and says God ‘hears my voice’ (Psalm 55:17).
passages.asks: Daniel kept praying just as he had done before. Ask what habits of faith you would keep if they became costly, and which you would quietly drop. And ask whether your prayers under pressure include thanks.

passages.t: Delivered at dawn, and the accusers thrown in
passages.happening:
At the first light of dawn the king hurries to the den (verse 19). He cries out in anguish, ‘O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?’ (verse 20).

Daniel answers, ‘My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, for I was found innocent in His sight, and I have done no wrong against you, O king’ (verse 22).

The king is overjoyed and has Daniel lifted out. No wound is found on him, ‘because he had trusted in his God’ (verse 23).

Then, at the king's command, the men who had falsely accused Daniel are thrown into the den, with their wives and children, and the lions overpower them before they reach the bottom (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The story is built on reversals. The officials looked for a charge and found only faithfulness. The king who signed the decree spent the day trying to save the man it condemned. The stone and the seals meant to make sure nothing about Daniel could change instead kept the evidence of his rescue. The accusers fall into the pit they dug.

Daniel's first words to the king are a greeting, and then a plain statement: he was found innocent before God and had done no wrong against the king. He was loyal to both, as far as loyalty to the king could go.

Lions were kept by Near Eastern kings. Assyrian palace reliefs show royal lion hunts, with lions released from cages, as a display of the king's power. The power the king kept in a pit could not touch the man God protected.

The punishment of the accusers with their wives and children reflects a practice of collective punishment known in the ancient world. The Law of Moses forbade it in Israel's own courts. The narrator reports it as Persian justice, not as a model.
passages.later: The Law said, ‘Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin’ (Deuteronomy 24:16). A psalm says of the wicked, ‘he has fallen into a pit of his own making’ (Psalm 7:15). And the letter to the Hebrews remembers those ‘who shut the mouths of lions’ (Hebrews 11:33).
passages.hard:
Why are the accusers' wives and children thrown to the lions?

This was the king's command, and it reflects the collective punishment some ancient rulers carried out. The narrator does not praise it. Israel's own law forbade it: children were not to be put to death for their parents (Deuteronomy 24:16), and the prophets repeated that each person answers for their own sin. The verse records what a Persian king did. It is not God's command and not a model.

The children in this verse had done nothing. The story does not call what happened to them right, and no reader should.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Daniel told the king he had done no wrong against him. Ask whether you can say that to the people you serve, as well as to God. And ask how you respond when someone who wronged you is punished, and whether you can still grieve what happened to the innocent with them.

passages.happening:
King Darius writes to the people of every nation and language in his land (verse 25). ‘I hereby decree that in every part of my kingdom, men are to tremble in fear before the God of Daniel’ (verse 26). ‘For He is the living God, and He endures forever; His kingdom will never be destroyed, and His dominion will never end’ (verse 26). ‘He delivers and rescues; He performs signs and wonders in the heavens and on the earth, for He has rescued Daniel from the power of the lions’ (verse 27).

‘So Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Darius calls Daniel's God the living God, in contrast to the idols of metal and wood that cannot see or hear, which Belshazzar had praised. The verb deliver, shezav, runs through this chapter and chapter 3, and here a Persian king confesses that Daniel's God delivers and rescues.

The decree restates the book's central claim in the mouth of a foreign ruler: his kingdom will never be destroyed. It echoes Daniel's words to Nebuchadnezzar in chapter 2, and it prepares for the vision of chapter 7, where that kingdom is given to one like a son of man.

This is the last of the court stories. Verse 28 can be read as Darius and Cyrus, two reigns, or, as D. J. Wiseman proposed, as the reign of Darius, that is, of Cyrus. Either way, Daniel outlasts Babylon, as chapter 1 said he would.
passages.later: Nebuchadnezzar had made the same confession after his humbling: ‘For His dominion is an everlasting dominion, and His kingdom endures from generation to generation’ (Daniel 4:34). And Daniel's next vision shows that kingdom given to ‘One like the Son of Man’ (Daniel 7:13). A psalm confesses the same: ‘Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom’ (Psalm 145:13).
passages.asks: A foreign king ended up confessing the God of the man he could not save. Ask who has seen your faith tested and what they would say about your God. And ask how you can serve faithfully under rulers who do not share your faith, as Daniel did for a lifetime.
